What sacrifice did Monsieur Loisel make for Mathilde's dress?
questions.answer: He gave her the four hundred francs he had saved to buy a gun and go shooting with friends at Nanterre the next summer, so that she could buy a gown for the ball.

questions.q: How does Mathilde's reaction to Madame Forestier's jewellery reveal her personality?
questions.answer: She tries everything, hesitates, and her heart throbs with desire when she sees the diamond necklace. She longs for it passionately, which shows her vanity and her craving to appear rich.

questions.q: Why was Mathilde always unhappy?
questions.answer: She felt that, being pretty and charming, she deserved a life of luxury. Her poor home, shabby furniture and plain food tortured her, and she envied rich people like her friend.

questions.q: Why was Mathilde a great success at the ball?
questions.answer: She was the prettiest woman there — elegant, graceful, smiling and wild with joy. Everyone admired her, all the men wanted to dance with her, and even the Minister noticed her.

questions.q: What did the Loisels do to find the necklace?
questions.answer: They searched the folds of her dress and cloak. Loisel retraced their route on foot and went to the police, the cab companies and the newspapers, offering a reward, but found nothing.

questions.q: How did the Loisels' life change after they bought the new necklace?
questions.answer: They dismissed the servant and moved to a garret. Mathilde did the heavy housework and haggled for every sou, while Loisel worked extra jobs. In ten years Mathilde became old, coarse and rough.

questions.q: Why did Mathilde tell Madame Forestier the truth at last?
questions.answer: The debts were paid and she felt proud of what they had endured. Meeting her friend, she wanted to explain why she looked so changed and to tell her of the sacrifice made for her necklace.

questions.q: What is the turning point in 'The Necklace'? How does it change Mathilde?
questions.answer: The loss of the necklace is the turning point. It forces Mathilde from dreams of luxury into ten years of poverty and toil. She becomes hard-working, brave and honest about her debt, though she loses her beauty and youth.

questions.q: 'Madame Loisel's sacrifice had all been in vain.' Comment.
questions.answer: The Loisels gave up ten years, their savings and Mathilde's beauty to replace a necklace that was only paste worth five hundred francs. Had she told her friend the truth, the suffering could have been avoided; pride and pretence cost them dearly.

or.answer: It warns against vanity and the desire to appear richer than we are. It teaches us to be content and honest: one moment of borrowed glory cost Mathilde ten years of hardship, which honesty could have prevented.

questions.q: Compare Mathilde and her husband.
questions.answer: Mathilde is vain and discontented, always dreaming of wealth. Loisel is simple and content, enjoying plain soup. He is patient and self-sacrificing — he gives up his savings, waits at the ball, and later works extra jobs for ten years without complaint.
